This book is not “world geography” — it is **Eritrea**. Outcomes: read the land’s story (rocks), water, climate, plants and animals, soils, how people make a living, and who lives where.

cards.title: 3.1 Introduction
body: **Climate** is the average condition of the atmosphere for thirty or more years.
The climate of a region is determined over a long period of study of climate elements and factors.
The elements of climate are temperature, precipitation, wind and pressure.
The factors are, latitude, ocean currents, topography, altitude, and more.
The climate of Eritrea is therefore determined by climate elements and factors that determine their patterns and distributions.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the average lapse rate in the troposphere, defining the temperature decrease per 1000 meters of altitude?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall the normal environmental lapse rate**
The standard environmental lapse rate in the troposphere is mathematically defined as a decrease of **$$6.5^\circ\text{C}$$ per $$1000\text{ m}$$** (or $$0.0065^\circ\text{C/m}$$).

**Step 2: Match with options**
The correct option is $$6.5^\circ\text{C}$$.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which altitudinal zone of climate is located between 700 meters and 2000 meters above sea level in Eritrea?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Check altitudinal divisions**
* Below $$700\text{ m}$$: Warm Tropical
* $$700\text{ m to } 2000\text{ m}$$: **Sub-tropical**
* Above $$2000\text{ m}$$: Cool Temperate

**Step 2: Conclude**
The zone is the Sub-tropical Zone.

cards.q: In a mountainous region, climate is mostly determined by
cards.why: In mountainous areas, altitude (height above sea level) is the primary climatic control. Temperature decreases by about 6.5°C for every 1,000 meters of ascent (lapse rate).

cards.title: 3.2 Factors of Climate in Eritrea
body: Latitude: Latitude is an imaginary line that runs from east to west or vice versa across the earth’s surface.
The sun’s radiation always oscillates within the tropics.
Cold prevails in those places that are found far from the tropical location.
Most neighboring countries of Eritrea experience high average daily temperatures because of their tropical locations.
The average daily temperature in tropical areas is estimated to be 20°C.

cards.title: Climate of Eritrea
body: Climate here is not “one country, one weather”. Altitude splits the map more than latitude does.

cards.title: Factors — L.A.R.S.W.
body: *Latitude, Altitude, Relief, Sea (Red Sea), Winds / ITCZ.* Height cools the highlands; the sea moistens and sometimes rains on the east; the ITCZ shift brings the main summer rains to the plateau and west.

steps.text: **Step 1.** In Eritrea, **altitude** (elevation above sea level) is the most significant factor affecting climate.

cards.title: 3.3 Temperature Distribution
body: Work in groups and preare a table of mean annual temperature distributions based on the altitudinal and latitudinal locations of five towns from the Lowlands and another five towns from the Highlands of Eritrea.
The six selected towns from the Highlands and the Lowlands are all located almost on the same latitudes.
The temperature of these towns ranges relative to their altitudinal differences.
The seasonal temperature distribution in Eritrea is however a function of latitude.
Between March 21 and September 23, the sun is overhead between the equator and the Tropic of Cancer.

cards.title: Altitude, not latitude, controls the temperature map
body: Towns at almost the same latitude have very different temperatures: Assab (10 m) averages about 30 °C, Tesseney (585 m) 28.5 °C, but Adi Ugri (2,022 m) only 17.4 °C and Segeneiti (2,203 m) 16.4 °C.

Mean annual temperature ranges from about **15 °C in the highlands** to **30 °C in the lowlands**; the Danakil can exceed 50 °C. The hottest months come as the sun moves overhead north of the equator (March–September).
The **diurnal range** is large (highland nights near 0 °C, days near 30 °C), but the **annual range** is small – under 10 °C – and larger in the lowlands than in the highlands.

cards.title: Estimate temperature from altitude
cards.problem: Massawa (near sea level) has a mean annual temperature of about 30 °C. Using a lapse rate of 6.5 °C per 1,000 m, estimate the mean temperature of Asmara (about 2,350 m). Why is the real value (about 16–17 °C) close to this?

steps.text: **Step 4: Compare.** The real mean (about 16–17 °C) is close, which shows that altitude, not latitude, controls Eritrea's temperature pattern.

cards.answer: About 15 °C (30 − 15.3); close to the observed value because temperature falls with altitude.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Assab (10 m) has a mean annual temperature of about 30 °C, while Adi Keih (2,423 m) has about 18 °C, though both lie near 13–15°N. What explains the difference?

options.B: Latitude: Assab is much nearer the equator
options.D: Altitude: temperature falls as height increases

cards.why:
**Step 1:** The towns lie at similar latitudes, so latitude cannot explain a 12 °C difference.

**Step 2:** Adi Keih is about 2,400 m higher.

**Step 3:** Temperature falls with altitude (about 6.5 °C per 1,000 m), so altitude explains it.

**Tip:** Use the key estimates: about 5.1 million people (2009), fertility about 5, 41.5% under 15, dependency ratio about 92, nine ethnic groups, densest in Maekel.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The diurnal range of temperature in the Eritrean highlands is ____.

options.B: large – nights can be near 0 °C and days near 30 °C
options.C: the same as in the Red Sea
options.D: larger than the annual range in every place by 50 °C

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Diurnal range = day maximum − night minimum.

**Step 2:** Clear, thin highland air heats quickly by day and loses heat fast at night.

**Step 3:** So the daily range is large, while the annual range is under 10 °C.

**Tip:** Use the key estimates: about 5.1 million people (2009), fertility about 5, 41.5% under 15, dependency ratio about 92, nine ethnic groups, densest in Maekel.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In which season does Eritrea usually record its highest temperatures?

options.A: When the sun is over the Tropic of Capricorn
options.D: When the overhead sun is north of the equator (March–September)

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Seasonal temperature follows the sun's position (latitude).

**Step 2:** Between March and September the sun is overhead in the northern hemisphere.

**Step 3:** Temperatures rise rapidly from March and April.

**Tip:** Use the key estimates: about 5.1 million people (2009), fertility about 5, 41.5% under 15, dependency ratio about 92, nine ethnic groups, densest in Maekel.

cards.title: 3.4 Winds in Eritrea
body: The north east trade winds and the south-westerly winds are the two principal winds dominant in Eritrea.

During winter season, the northeast trade winds blow across Eritrea on their way to the low pressure area or a convergence zone (Intertropical Convergence Zone), which is located around southern Africa.
The south westerly winds are wet as they originate from the Atlantic Ocean.
The Anabatic (upslope) winds which develop during day time for example move up slopes due to greater heating of the valley sides compared with the valley floor.
The Anabatic (upslope) winds move up slopes of the eastern and western slopes and meet the prevailing winds on the top of the plateau surface.

cards.title: Seasonal and local winds
body: **Winter:** dry **north-east trade winds** blow from Asia and Arabia towards the ITCZ, then over southern Africa. Crossing the Red Sea they pick up a little moisture, giving winter rain to the coast and eastern escarpment.
**Summer:** wet **south-westerly winds** from the Atlantic (south-east trades deflected by the earth's rotation) blow towards the ITCZ north of Eritrea and bring the main kiremti rains.
**Local winds:** by day, heated slopes produce **anabatic (upslope)** winds; at night, cooled air drains down as **katabatic (downslope)** winds. Both affect local temperature and rainfall.

cards.title: 3.5 Rainfall in Eritrea
body: The word rainfall is used to denote that part of the precipitation that falls on the ground in the form of large water droplets.
Rainfall is expressed in millimeters (mm) or inches for a day, month, year, and other time distinction.
Rainfall is seasonal and varies from year to year in Eritrea.
The variability of rainfall amount and distribution in Eritrea is mainly caused by the location of the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone and its associated wind circulations.
The **Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone** is a belt of low pressure area that marks the boundary between the two opposing trade wind belts.

cards.title: Three rainy seasons
body: **Spring rain (March):** light rain from moist air from the Gulf of Aden and Indian Ocean as the ITCZ moves north.
**Summer rain (kiremti, June–September):** the ITCZ lies north of Eritrea; south-westerly winds from the Gulf of Guinea and Congo basin bring the largest rains to the highlands and western lowlands.
**Winter rain (November–March):** north-east trade winds bring rain to the Red Sea coast and the eastern escarpment; the Green Belt (Filfil, Solomuna) can get up to 1,000 mm or more.
Rainfall increases from north to south: Asmara about 547 mm, Adi Ugri 572 mm, Adi Quala 687 mm; the coastal plains get only about 50–180 mm.

cards.title: 3.6 Humidity
body: **Humidity** refers to the amount of moisture or water vapor in the atmosphere.
Humidity can be expressed in absolute or relative terms.
The weight of water vapor in a given volume of air is called **absolute humidity**.
**Specific humidity** is the weight of moisture per parcel of air.
**Relative humidity** is the ratio between absolute humidity and saturation at a given temperature.

cards.title: Exam sticky notes
body: - Escarpment is the green belt

cards.title: Humidity in Eritrea at a glance
body: **Absolute humidity** is the mass of water vapour in a given volume of air; **specific humidity** is the mass of vapour per mass of air; **relative humidity (RH)** compares the vapour present with the most the air could hold at that temperature, as a percentage.

RH is highest along the Red Sea coast (about 60%, from Assab to north of Massawa) and highest of all from the coast up into the Green Belt (about 75%). It is lowest in the western lowlands near the Sudan border.

Seasonally, RH is highest from **August to November** and lowest from **January to April**. Warm air can hold more vapour, so the same amount of vapour gives a lower RH on a hot afternoon than on a cool morning.

cards.title: 3.7 Potential Evapo-Transpiration
body: **Evapo-transpiration** is the loss of moisture in the atmosphere.
The moisture is lost as evaporation from the soil surface and transpiration from vegetation.
The highest amount of moisture lost in the form of evaporation and transpiration from an area where the amount of water supply is unlimited is called Potential Evapo-transpiration (PET).
Evapo-transpiration greatly affects the amount of surface and ground water supplies.
Evapo-transpiration and altitude show inverse relationship.

cards.title: Potential Evapo-Transpiration
body: **Humidity** is higher on the coast; inland air is often dry. High PET (potential evapotranspiration) in the hot lowlands “eats” rain before crops see it.

cards.title: Reading the rainfall and PET table
body: PET falls as altitude rises because highland temperatures are lower.
**Lowland stations:** Assab rain 45 mm / PET 1,974 mm; Massawa 191 / 1,944 mm; Akordat 309 / 2,051 mm; Tesseney 348 / 2,064 mm – huge water deficits.
**Highland stations:** Asmara 547 / 1,507 mm; Adi Keih 484 / 533 mm – Adi Keih's rain nearly matches its PET, so its deficit is small.

cards.title: 3.8 Rainfall Deficit in Eritrea
body: The most common explanations given for such seasonality or variability of rainfall is the instability of the Inter-tropical Convergence Zone both in time and space.
Even if excess water reaches the ground surface, it has routes to follow, either to disappear or accumulate somewhere else.
Once precipitation reaches the ground, some of it evaporates, and the remainder either seeps into the ground or runs off as rivers and streams to the sea.

The ratio of the portion that infiltrates the earth’s surface to the portion that runs off depends on the intensity of rainfall, and on the vegetation, topography, and physical properties of the surface.
Information from weather stations around the country indicates that inadequate rainfall and high evapo-transpiration remain the major problem for crop production in Eritrea.

cards.title: Rainfall Deficit in Eritrea
body: **Rain:** main season is summer (kiremti) on the plateau and west. The eastern escarpment can also catch winter / coastal rains — that is why it stays greener. Totals are low and unreliable → **rainfall deficit** when rain < potential evapotranspiration.

cards.title: What a rainfall deficit means for Eritrea
body: A region has a **rainfall (water) deficit** when its rainfall is less than its **potential evapotranspiration (PET)** – the water that would evaporate from the soil and transpire from plants if water were always available. Deforestation and misuse of land make the deficit worse.

Eritrea's rainfall is **seasonal and variable** because the **Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ)** shifts unevenly from year to year. Massawa, for example, receives only about 190 mm of rain a year but has a PET of about 1,900 mm.

When rain falls, part evaporates, part soaks into the ground and part runs off. The share that infiltrates depends on rainfall intensity, vegetation, slope and soil. Heavy storms on bare, steep land mostly run off.

Effects: low soil moisture, falling groundwater, poor harvests and shortages of domestic water. Eritrea suffered major droughts in **1972 and 1984**. Responses include dams and ponds, terraces, tree planting, water harvesting and drought-tolerant crops.

cards.title: Decide whether a place has a water deficit
cards.problem: A station records 450 mm of rain a year and a potential evapotranspiration of 1,300 mm a year. Does it have a rainfall deficit? How large is it, and what does it mean for farming?

steps.text: **Step 1: Compare.** Deficit exists when rainfall < PET: 450 < 1,300, so yes.
**Step 3: Ratio.** Rainfall covers only 450 ÷ 1,300 ≈ 35% of the water demand.
**Step 4: Meaning.** Crops will suffer moisture stress unless water is stored or irrigated; drought-tolerant crops, water harvesting and soil cover help.

cards.answer: Yes; the deficit is 850 mm a year (rain meets only about 35% of PET), so farming needs irrigation, water harvesting or drought-tolerant crops.

**Step 2:** If the supply is less than the potential loss, the region lacks water.

**Step 3:** That condition is a rainfall (water) deficit.

tips.text: Climate is the average weather condition of a place computed for long period of time. It is expressed through its elements like temperature, precipitation and pressure and winds. These elements are in turn controlled by several factors.
Latitude and altitude, as controls of weather and climate, are the two most important factors that determine the climate of Eritrea.
Since it has a tropical location, one can expect high temperature and precipitation to prevail throughout Eritrea.
Nonetheless, due to the influence of altitude, the amount and distribution of the elements of climate are not uniformly distributed in Eritrea.
Rainfall is seasonal and concentrated mostly during summer season.
The amount and distribution is also not reliable. As a result, the country has a water deficit.

questions.q: Which belt is typically the greenest?
why: Answer A: Eastern escarpment
The eastern escarpment receives rain from moist Red Sea air (winter rains) as well as some summer rain, so it has the densest vegetation; the Danakil floor and western lowlands are dry.

similar.q: In winter, Eritrea is under the influence of the  A) Westerly Winds.  B) Southeast Trade Winds.  C) Northeast Trade Winds.  D) A and B.  E) B and C.
similar.a: C. Northeast Trade Winds. — During winter season, the northeast trade winds blow across Eritrea on their way to the low pressure area south of the equator; in summer the south-westerly winds dominate. Answer: C.

questions.q: The temperature at which the **point of saturation** is reached is called _________.
why: The **Dew point** is the specific temperature to which air must be cooled (at constant pressure) for it to become saturated with water vapor and begin condensing into liquid water.

questions.q: The planetary winds that converge or meet at the Doldrums are the
why: The Doldrums (Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone or ITCZ) is a low-pressure belt around the equator where the Northeast and Southeast **Trade Winds** meet and rise.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: ITCZ during winter season is located in the

options.A: North of Equator and South of Eritrea

why: The **Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ)** follows the apparent movement of the sun. During the Northern Hemisphere's winter (December/January), the sun is overhead in the Southern Hemisphere (Tropic of Capricorn), causing the ITCZ to shift **South of the equator**.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: The Eastern escarpment and the coastal areas of Eritrea receive **winter rainfall** by
why: During the winter months (November to February), the North East Trade Winds blow from the Asian landmass across the Red Sea. As they cross the sea, they pick up moisture and bring rain to the Eritrean coast and the eastern escarpment.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: The two most dominant winds in Eritrea that bring rainfall in summer season and winter season **respectively** are the

options.A: northeast trade winds and southeast trade winds.
options.B: northeast trade winds and south-westerly winds.
options.C: southeast trade winds and south-westerly winds.
options.D: south-westerly winds and northeast trade winds.

why: Eritrea's rainfall pattern is bimodal. Summer rains (July–August) in the highlands and western lowlands are brought by the **South-westerly winds** (monsoons). Winter rains (November–February) on the eastern escarpment and coastal plains are brought by the **Northeast trade winds** blowing over the Red Sea.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: The local name for spring rainfall in Eritrea is
why: In Eritrea, the spring rains (March to May) are locally known as 'Azmera'. They are crucial for land preparation before the main summer rains.

why: Assab, located on the Red Sea coast in the Southern Red Sea region, is known for having one of the highest mean annual temperatures in Eritrea due to its coastal lowland position and proximity to the Afar Depression.

why: The dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated (reaches 100% relative humidity). At this temperature, water vapor starts to condense into liquid water (dew).

questions.q: The ability of air to hold moisture largely depends on
why: Warm air has a higher capacity to hold water vapor than cold air. As air temperature increases, its ability to hold moisture also increases.

questions.q: Which of the following cities have the highest humidity?
why: Humidity is highest in coastal areas due to their proximity to a large body of water (the Red Sea) and high rates of evaporation. Assab and Massawa are Eritrea's primary coastal cities.
